newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin rules out rushed changes to constitution.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin rules out rushed changes to constitution.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, making his first radio address since he fell ill with pneumonia, on Friday ruled out hasty constitutional amendments sought by his political foes to reduce his powers or oust him.

"Amendments and additions can be made to (the constitution) but you should not rush this. It must be a natural process," Yeltsin said, speaking clearly but slowly and with a slightly hoarse voice in a six-minute address.

The 66-year-old president, who is still recovering from the pneumonia he suffered last month, reaffirmed his government's commitment to pay all pension arrears and again made clear he would not let the rebel Chechnya region secede.
"There can be no one-sided decisions in our relations," said Yeltsin.
The president has had at least two heart attacks, he had heart surgery last November and he spent 12 days in hospital with pneumonia last month.
Communist opposition leaders are seeking to oust Yeltsin on health grounds and the lower house of parliament was due to debate a resolution on their proposals on Friday.
Regulations for removing a sick president are vague and the opposition's chances of ousting him are minimal.
Yeltsin's poor health has prompted concern over the constitution, which was approved in a nationwide referendum in December 1993 and which gives the president vast powers.

Proposals for constitutional changes include allowing Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to serve as president until the end of Yeltsin's scheduled term if the president dies in office, reducing the president's powers, setting up a state council to govern or having the next president chosen by Yeltsin.

Yeltsin last made a full address to the Russian people in December. Russian television has shown him several times since then at meetings with Russian and visiting foreign leaders. He has looked thin and sometimes had a glazed look.

Turning to Chechnya, Yeltsin said the breakaway region's newly-elected President Aslan Maskhadov should concentrate on sorting out problems within Chechnya, including ensuring good relations between Chechens and ethnic Russians who live there.
"A great responsibility lies with the leadership of Chechnya," Yeltsin said.
Touching on unpaid pensions, which has caused widespread anger, Yeltsin said the government would pay pensions on time from now on and that all pension arrears would be settled.
